rv.q: Skeleton Crew does all that and more, finding hope in the unlikeliest of places, like a cluttered, ramshackle break room of a noisy, about-to-fail factory in an about-to-fail city like Detroit.
Morisseau has penned a true ensemble piece highlighted by individuals who are flawed, relatable and vastly human.

Morisseau understands, and in this finely wrought monologue conveys concisely, that blue-collar work can be as rewarding, and inspiring of loyalty and pride, as better-paying, more prestigious and less physically demanding jobs.
In the drafty hall, Morisseau’s carefully banked fires start to flicker.

It’s so adroitly built and written — and, in the Manhattan Theater Club production that opened on Wednesday, so beautifully staged and acted — that you hardly have time to decide, until its brisk two hours have passed, whether it’s a comedy or a tragedy.

If some of the grit has been lost in Skeleton Crew's refurbished Broadway form, which also includes flashy video effects, Morisseau's play remains firmly based in the lives and evocative language of its characters, whom Santiago-Hudson treats with the respect they deserve.
Morisseau’s dad was right: She knew what she was doing, and definitely got somewhere good.
She knows how to get my motor running.

It's that pride that Morisseau wants to pay tribute to, and in a play that might have nothing but bad awaiting its characters as the huge thumb of capitalism hovers over their heads, we're left with a little bit of hope.
Ruben Santiago-Hudson’s absorbing production has finally officially opened and was well worth the wait.

Rashad is fantastic as the “tough as bricks” Faye, and Dirden—featured in Santiago-Hudson’s gorgeous revivals of August Wilson’s The Piano Lesson (2012) and Jitney (2016), not to mention in Detroit ’67 (2013)—is simply spectacular as the buttoned-up Reggie.
Morriseau has created a brilliant, modern workplace tragedy, masterfully attuned to the ways the American Dream has made sleepwalkers of us all.
Morisseau’s well-built and affecting play gives us a strikingly relevant portrait of an oppressive economy and those struggling to find their way through it.

If I don’t personally find this the right time to mount this play, and I see stumbles in the Broadway production compared to the Off-Broadway original, this is still a solid production of a worthwhile play.
Despite the fine acting by the ensemble, Skeleton Crew proves a well-meaning, respectable play that ultimately underwhelms.
Their positivism sparks a convenient conflict involving the disillusioned Des, but it also establishes him as the only one with a grip on reality.
She’s also left the door open so that white audiences can grasp an honest view of what Black people talk about when white folks aren’t around, making Skeleton Crew a must-see.

This rich theatrical evening is directed with skill, flair, and heart by the versatile Ruben Santiago-Hudson (who is having an exciting season on Broadway, having just come off a successful run of Lackawanna Blues ).

Skeleton Crew solidly creates a sobering and powerful portrait of camaraderie and survival, pounded out on the line, in the writing and direction, as economic destruction seems to be waiting out in the cold, trying to freeze them out.
This is theatre that reminds you why theater is the closest thing to hallowed ground we have.
The script by Dominique Morisseau is beautifully written with lyric language and imagery.

cn.t: Critics praise Morisseau's compassionate, eloquently written drama about Detroit auto workers facing plant closure, with stellar performances led by Rashad. Some find it stronger on atmosphere than dramatic tension, though most laud its emotional generosity.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
